title_en: Every Xbox console generation sorted by release date
title_fa: Every Xbox console generation sorted by release date
excerpt_en: Microsoft debuted the Xbox in 2001, and there's quite a lot to look back on from the quarter-century since the company got into gaming.
excerpt_fa: Microsoft debuted the Xbox in 2001, and there's quite a lot to look back on from the quarter-century since the company got into gaming.
content_en:
Every Xbox console generation sorted by release date
Celebrate 25 years of Xbox with a trip down memory lane.
Since taking a crack at gaming in 2001, Microsoft has rolled out nine distinct Xbox variations across four generations (not including different SKUs like the Xbox 360 Arcade). From the jump, the line has introduced new ideas that (literally) changed the game, like revolutionizing online console gaming, introducing achievements and launching a subscription-based game library with Xbox Game Pass.
With it being 25 years since the first console and its little shooter game about aliens hit shelves, it's a great chance to take a trip down memory lane. While details about the next Xbox are still up in the air, now's the time to reminisce. Let's start at the top, from the days of the Duke controller to "everything is an Xbox."
Xbox | November 15, 2001
In 2001, the original $300 Xbox went toe-to-toe with Sony and Nintendo, who had released the PS2 and GameCube in the US within a 13 month-period. The sales affirm that the PS2 was by far this generation's most popular console — and the best-selling console of all time, in fact. But Microsoft deserves tons of credit for the high standard it set for online gaming with Xbox Live, which launched in late 2002.
With just $50 a year and an active internet connection, gamers could play Halo: Combat Evolved and more with friends or randoms; the exclusive series alone was often enough to draw people into buying an Xbox. According to a Microsoft press release from 2003, the service had over 300,000 subscribers within four months, outperforming the PS2's network adapters by nearly 50 percent in subscriber count.
By mid-2005, a few months after Halo 2 was released the holiday season prior, the service had a whopping two million subscribers. And while that's wildly impressive, it wasn't the biggest news to come from Xbox that year.
Xbox 360 | November 22, 2005
The Xbox 360 launched in 2005 in two configurations. The $400 Premium had a wireless controller and a detachable 20GB hard drive pre-loaded with a few goodies. Meanwhile, the $300 Core had a wired controller and no hard drive, forcing owners to buy one separately or use a memory card for save data.
After the PlayStation 3 and Wii came out in 2006, Microsoft upped the ante in 2007 with the pictured Elite configuration. It featured a matte black finish, a 120GB hard drive and, arguably most important of all, an HDMI port.
Then in 2010, Microsoft released the 360 Slim, tackling the original's infamous overheating problem that often led to the Red Ring of Death. This revamped model had a whole new cooling system and up to 320GB of storage. Ultimately, Microsoft ushered this famed generation out with the 360 E in June 2013, introducing a sleeker design just months before the Xbox One arrived.
Even with the Red Ring, Microsoft's second-gen console remains its best-selling ever, with at least 84 million units sold. This generation rolled out features like achievements and Gamerscore, rewarding progress and often giving a reason to revisit games. Speaking of which, the Xbox 360's now-iconic exclusive games may be coming to PC, giving us a chance to replay hits like Halo 3, Fable II, Gears of War and Forza Motorsport 2.
Although the Wii is often viewed as the biggest reason for motion-control gaming going mainstream, Microsoft's Kinect tried taking the idea in a new direction in 2010. It tracked the player's whole body with a camera, rather than a sensor bar only tracking a remote. While it was optional to start, Microsoft had different plans when the next generation arrived.
Xbox One | November 22, 2013
Microsoft gambled out of the gate when it revealed the Xbox One in summer 2013, planning to bundle the $499 console with a Kinect 2.0 and forcing players to keep the motion camera plugged in. Before the console hit shelves in November, the company reversed this and asserted that Kinect wouldn't be necessary, to the delight of many. Come 2014, the company dropped the Xbox One's price to $400 and stopped bundling the two.
The console also answered a long-running taunt from PS3 owners with its built-in Blu-ray player. It also came with a 500GB hard drive and a slightly redesigned controller with new thumbsticks, impulse triggers and other upgrades.
Over the generation, the Xbox One got a few hardware upgrades. The $399 Xbox One S arrived in 2016 with no dedicated Kinect port. Failed accessories aside, this iteration notably brought 4K support to the table, now featuring a 4K Blu-ray player, 4K streaming capabilities and 1080p upscaling. Plus, it was 40 percent smaller than the huge original model.
Then in 2017, the $499 Xbox One X became Microsoft's first console to deliver native 4K gameplay, with HDR support to match. To make the most of this, Microsoft rolled out Xbox One X Enhanced versions of many titles, offering higher resolutions and frame rates. But since not every re-released game took full advantage, native 4K support varied by title.
Xbox Series X and S | November 10, 2020
The Xbox Series X was unveiled in 2019, a year before hitting shelves for the 2020 holiday season at $500. Self-positioned as Microsoft's fastest and most powerful console to date, it promised ultra-low latency and native 4K gaming that could max out at 120FPS, as well as eventual support for 8K capabilities (though 8K is essentially dead now).
A year after the Series X was announced, and just two months before its release date, Xbox revealed the $300 Series S, a much cheaper take on the console. Since it lacks a disc drive, this digital-only model is better suited for Game Pass subscribers and anyone who doesn't care to buy physical copies. Microsoft says resolution is the key difference between models: the Series S maxes out at 1440p and can only upscale games, not offer true 4K gaming capabilities.
These days, after several price increases, the Series S starts at $500 for the 512GB system, while the Series X is $750 for the...

title_en: Customers at major banks report difficulty accessing accounts online
title_fa: Customers at major banks report difficulty accessing accounts online
excerpt_en: Representatives from the companies say this is a technical problem and not a cyberattack.
excerpt_fa: Representatives from the companies say this is a technical problem and not a cyberattack.
content_en:
Customers at major banks report difficulty accessing accounts online
The companies say this is a technical problem and not a cyberattack.
Customers of multiple banks and financial services are reportedly experiencing service disruptions today. Chase, Bank of America, US Bank and Wells Fargo were the top four services with issues reported on Down Detector at 3PM ET, but Zelle, Capitol One, PNC, JPMorgan and Truist were seeing spikes in unavailability. The number of reports began increasing for some banks around 10AM ET, while others didn't begin spiking until the afternoon.
A representative from Chase told the Associated Press that customers might be seeing slower transaction times "due to a technical issue," and added that it was not a cybersecurity problem. The publication also heard from a spokesperson for US Bank who said clients might see delays for sending or receiving payments through Zelle.
The service interruptions for these financial institutions follows on multiple headline-grabbing technical issues. Several Microsoft services went down on November 12. The following day the US Federal Administration Authority issued a ground stop for all flights in the country following a problem with air traffic control equipment.

title_en: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
title_fa: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
excerpt_en: California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a "dangerous...
excerpt_fa: California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a "dangerous...
content_en:
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.
California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. excerpt_fa: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. "I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer," Altman said today. "I think the home tinkering is...
content_en:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”
Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’
Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’
The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday.
Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month, saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.”
AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”
Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying:
“The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”
Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

title_en: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers

excerpt_fa: Constellation Energy - America's largest operator of nuclear power plants - does not share Wall Street's concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company's third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word,...
content_en:
Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
They may have a point.
They may have a point.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.

title_en: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
title_fa: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
excerpt_en: Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of...
excerpt_fa: Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of...
content_en:
Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year.
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

title_en: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
title_fa: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
excerpt_en: The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.
excerpt_fa: The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.
content_en:
OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office, alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public.
At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise, in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident, OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”
The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.
The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems, DseWiki, the Wikimedia Foundation, and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.
The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure.
“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”
The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.
It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users, particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.
In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”
In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.
“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
Updated 12:23 p.m. PT: Added OpenAI statement.

title_en: California sues OpenAI after that Hugging Face rogue hacking incident
title_fa: California sues OpenAI after that Hugging Face rogue hacking incident
excerpt_en: State AG Rob Bonta has accused the company of making AI agents "without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect" users.
excerpt_fa: State AG Rob Bonta has accused the company of making AI agents "without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect" users.
content_en:
California sues OpenAI after that Hugging Face rogue hacking incident
State AG Rob Bonta has accused the company of making AI agents “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” users.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Bonta has accused the entity of developing AI models "without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public."
The suit centers on the now famous Hugging Face incident, in which dozens of AI agents created by OpenAI reportedly went rogue and hacked computer systems at another company. The organization says its agents hacked Hugging Face on their own after escaping confinement and has since called for "stronger safeguards and defensive tools."
We're suing OpenAI for its testing and development of dangerous AI models without adequate safeguards.
In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law.https://t.co/SKCO15uzHx pic.twitter.com/IZCAnVm2ju
— Rob Bonta (@AGRobBonta) November 16, 2026
Bonta, however, alleges the attack was "entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI's choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight." It is worth noting that we don't even know exactly which models were involved in the hack. OpenAI just says it was a combination that included GPT-5.6 but also an "even more capable pre-release model."
The AG's office has accused the ChatGPT maker of creating a "public nuisance" by failing to secure the testing of its models. Bonta went on to allege that this represents a violation of California's Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits businesses in the state from engaging in illegal or fraudulent practices.
"The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," he said in a statement. "In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law."
OpenAI has yet to comment on the suit. It wrote in a blog post back in August that "without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls" and "take dangerous actions that no human directed."
California's suit looks to mandate some of those proper safeguards, as it would force OpenAI to implement monitoring systems and secure testing environments. Bonta is seeking civil penalties of $2,500 per violation.

title_en: The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
title_fa: The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
excerpt_en: If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $329 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart,...
excerpt_fa: If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $329 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart,...
content_en:
If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $329 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, beating the October Prime Day price by $20. If you prefer a larger size, the 46mm model is on sale for $379 ($70 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, which is also $20 lower than the previous best price.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
Apple’s latest smartwatch introduces AI-powered audio features, redesigned health sensors, and faster charging.
Apple’s latest smartwatch introduces AI-powered audio features, redesigned health sensors, and faster charging.
The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around.
It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day.

title_en: Which Google Pixel phone is most similar to the Galaxy S26+?
title_fa: Which Google Pixel phone is most similar to the Galaxy S26+?
excerpt_en: Trying to choose between the Google Pixel 11 Pro and Samsung Galaxy S26+? We break down the specs, cameras and prices to help find the best one for you.
excerpt_fa: Trying to choose between the Google Pixel 11 Pro and Samsung Galaxy S26+? We break down the specs, cameras and prices to help find the best one for you.
content_en:
Which Google Pixel phone is most similar to the Galaxy S26+?
Google Pixel is considered the cleanest Android experience, but which model holds up against the Samsung Galaxy S26+?
On paper, Samsung's Galaxy S26 and Google's Pixel 11 family of smartphones look surprisingly alike. You get three models to choose from on either side of the divide, but pit the two companies' offerings head-to-head and you'll find that the comparison isn't as straightforward.
For instance, the Galaxy S26+ specifically sits in the middle of Samsung's flagship lineup. However, you'll need to step up to Google's top-of-the-line Pixel 11 Pro XL for a direct equivalent. The Pixel 11 Pro also comes close to offering the same experience, but it makes a few tradeoffs while undercutting the Galaxy S26+ on price by a small margin.
With that in mind, here's how the Pixel 11 series stacks up against the Galaxy S26+, the middle child of Samsung's flagship smartphone lineup. Let's start with the Pixel 11 Pro, which seems like a natural competitor to the Galaxy S26+ as they each occupy the middle slot in Google and Samsung's flagship portfolios, respectively. Look a bit closer, though, and you'll find some fairly significant differences between them.
Galaxy S26+ vs Pixel 11 Pro: A surprisingly big difference
Samsung's Galaxy S26+ is a fairly large smartphone — it packs a 6.7-inch display that's only 0.2 inches smaller than the S26 Ultra. The Pixel 11 Pro, meanwhile, is quite compact by modern smartphone standards as we found out in our review. It has a 6.3-inch display, which is exactly the same as the base Galaxy S26.
If you don't mind the screen size difference, though, the Pixel 11 Pro is nearly an even match for the Galaxy S26+ in many other ways. In fact, Google's Pro phone offers a brighter display and more capable set of cameras. One major caveat is that the Galaxy S26 series enjoys a healthy lead in terms of raw performance. Google's Tensor G6 is primarily designed to support AI workloads, while the Galaxy S26's Snapdragon Elite Gen 5 — quoted as the "world's faster mobile system-on-a-chip" at launch by manufacturer Qualcomm — delivers considerably more processing and graphics horsepower (as does its international Exynos 2600 chip).
Still, the Pixel 11's Tensor G6 can handle day-to-day tasks and even multitasking just fine. The Galaxy S26+ simply pulls ahead in gaming, video editing and other resource-intensive applications. But on the plus side, the Pixel 11 Pro's $1,099 price tag undercuts the Galaxy S26+'s $1,199 MSRP.
The Pixel 11 Pro XL is the closest match to the Galaxy S26+
If you find the Pixel 11 Pro too small, Google's larger Pro XL model is a much closer match to the Galaxy S26+. Its 6.8-inch display is a touch larger than the 6.7-inch panel found on Samsung's middleweight flagship. Google also equips the Pixel 11 Pro with superior camera hardware, offering a 50MP primary lens, 48MP ultrawide and 48MP telephoto with 5x optical zoom. The Galaxy S26+ has a 50MP main camera but only a 12MP ultrawide and 10MP telephoto with 3x optical zoom. Samsung reserves its best optical sensors for the top-of-the-line Galaxy S26 Ultra.
At $1,299, the Pixel 11 Pro XL is $100 more than the Galaxy S26+'s $1,199 MSRP. Because Samsung's flagship line has been on the market longer, you're more likely to score a discount on the Galaxy S26+. You'll also notice a major difference in hand: the largest Pixel weighs a hefty 8 ounces (226 grams) compared to the 6.7-ounce (190-gram) Galaxy S26+. It's easy to notice the difference when holding the phones in the real world. The Pixel 11 Pro XL feels reassuringly hefty, but that feeling can eventually turn to fatigue during extended use.

title_en: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
title_fa: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
excerpt_en: Apple's latest iOS 27.3 developer beta introduces a limited face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo, alongside other improvements.
excerpt_fa: Apple's latest iOS 27.3 developer beta introduces a limited face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo, alongside other improvements.
content_en:
One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup.
With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade.
To be clear, this feature is not Face ID.
Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay.
The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is closed. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity.
The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it.
Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images.
The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness.
Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month.
Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a web page, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify.
Apple is also expanding access to Apple News puzzles for News+ subscribers in Australia, the U.K., and for French-Canadian users. Australian News+ subscribers will get access to a daily quick crossword, crossword mini, and Sudoku, as well as Apple’s original puzzles, Quartiles and Emoji Game. U.K. users will get the quick crossword, the crossword mini, and Sudoku, while French-Canadian subscribers will get access to Apple’s original puzzles.
The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete.

title_en: Google Maps' chatbot can find appointments and call to book them for you
title_fa: Google Maps' chatbot can find appointments and call to book them for you
excerpt_en: The Ask Maps chatbot is also expanding to more than 30 additional countries across Europe.
excerpt_fa: The Ask Maps chatbot is also expanding to more than 30 additional countries across Europe.
content_en:
Google Maps' chatbot can find appointments and call to book them for you
The Ask Maps chatbot is also expanding to more than 30 additional countries across Europe.
Google has announced several updates for Ask Maps, a Gemini-powered chatbot for Google Maps that debuted earlier this year. It's now capable of finding appointments (such as for beauty, pet care and auto and home repair) and calling local businesses to book them for you. If you prompt the chatbot to search for an appointment, Ask Maps might request some additional details before showing you available slots.
On a similar note, you can ask the chatbot to look for open tables at restaurants you've saved to your lists. For instance, you can request a table for a certain number of people within the next hour and it'll pull up what's available.
Appointment help: For last-minute appointments, Ask Maps can check open slots online, or even call local businesses for you. Really handy for errands like haircuts, nail appointments, pet grooming, home repair, or car maintenance. pic.twitter.com/35BdaL8etb
— Miriam Daniel (@miriamkdaniel) November 16, 2026
There are updated trip planning features as well. You can use Ask Maps to plan a road trip with stops based on your interests and it'll generate a schedule you can modify and share with others or export to Google Docs.
Before you head out, you'll be able to view "know before you go" info about the weather, electric vehicle charging spots, tolls and possible delays. When you hit the road, you can use Ask Maps to bring up the itinerary and display all the details you need for your route. You'll be able to modify your itinerary on the fly as well, which may come in useful if you change your mind about what to have for lunch, for instance.
Google is making these Ask Maps updates available on Android and iOS starting today. The list search and travel itinerary features can be used anywhere that Ask Maps is up and running. The appointment booking and "know before you go" route advice will only be accessible in the US at first, with availability in more regions to follow soon.
The company is also expanding the number of countries where Ask Maps is available to more than 200. It's bringing the chatbot to more than 30 additional countries across Europe, including the UK, Germany and Spain.

Google Maps' chatbot can find appointments and call to book them for you
The Ask Maps chatbot is also expanding to more than 30 additional countries across Europe.
Google has announced several updates for Ask Maps, a Gemini-powered chatbot for Google Maps that debuted earlier this year. It's now capable of finding appointments (such as for beauty, pet care and auto and home repair) and calling local businesses to book them for you. If you prompt the chatbot to search for an appointment, Ask Maps might request some additional details before showing you available slots.
On a similar note, you can ask the chatbot to look for open tables at restaurants you've saved to your lists. For instance, you can request a table for a certain number of people within the next hour and it'll pull up what's available.
Appointment help: For last-minute appointments, Ask Maps can check open slots online, or even call local businesses for you. Really handy for errands like haircuts, nail appointments, pet grooming, home repair, or car maintenance. pic.twitter.com/35BdaL8etb
— Miriam Daniel (@miriamkdaniel) November 16, 2026
There are updated trip planning features as well. You can use Ask Maps to plan a road trip with stops based on your interests and it'll generate a schedule you can modify and share with others or export to Google Docs.
Before you head out, you'll be able to view "know before you go" info about the weather, electric vehicle charging spots, tolls and possible delays. When you hit the road, you can use Ask Maps to bring up the itinerary and display all the details you need for your route. You'll be able to modify your itinerary on the fly as well, which may come in useful if you change your mind about what to have for lunch, for instance.
Google is making these Ask Maps updates available on Android and iOS starting today. The list search and travel itinerary features can be used anywhere that Ask Maps is up and running. The appointment booking and "know before you go" route advice will only be accessible in the US at first, with availability in more regions to follow soon.
The company is also expanding the number of countries where Ask Maps is available to more than 200. It's bringing the chatbot to more than 30 additional countries across Europe, including the UK, Germany and Spain.

title_en: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
title_fa: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
excerpt_en: Trump contradicted his own government's intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.
excerpt_fa: Trump contradicted his own government's intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.
content_en:
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”
Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy.
“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”
Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.
The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.
Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.
“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

title_en: Improve your Amazon Kindle experience by doing these simple things
title_fa: Improve your Amazon Kindle experience by doing these simple things
excerpt_en: If you love the convenience of a Kindle but miss the feel of having a physical book in your hands, we have some tips for you.
excerpt_fa: If you love the convenience of a Kindle but miss the feel of having a physical book in your hands, we have some tips for you.
content_en:
Improve your Amazon Kindle experience by doing these simple things
Changing a few settings can make your Kindle feel more book-like.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
As ebook and ereader technologies continue to evolve, the actual process of reading a book on a device has also begun to take on some rather fascinating changes. Though there are always going to be detractors who prefer the act of holding a physical book, products like the Amazon Kindle have done their part in making the hobby more accessible than ever before.
Sometimes, though, you may come to the realization that the sterile, almost inhuman feeling of reading a book on a Kindle can harsh your cozy vibe. It's something that has plagued the digital book market for years, but thanks to a few handy little upgrades and modifications, you can make reading a Kindle book feel like something far more compelling.
The ebook scene is one that's got its fair share of competitors, but if you are reading a lot of digital books, it's likely that you have one of Amazon's range of Kindle models. To help spiff up your days catching up on reading, we've put together a comprehensive look at how you can make that experience even more enjoyable.
How to make a Kindle feel more like a physical book
If you already have a Kindle, or have plans to get one, you may want to know which models can do certain things from within the ereader itself. For changing how the Kindle looks and operates on its screen, Amazon offers quite a lot of customization that you may have never even messed around with before.
Buy a cover that resembles a book
A common complaint about digital books is that they are, in fact, digital books. The actual weight and feeling of reading a book that's in your hands is gone, but if you're willing to part with some cash, you can change that up pretty easily.
They're a bit on the pricier side, but there are so many cases online that can make the Kindle look like a book. There are some genuinely charming and beautiful designs, many of which can help evoke the texts of yesteryear that made you fall in love with books to begin with. A quick Amazon search for "Kindle book cover" will get you started.
Change the font
When you have a book open on your Kindle, you have a lot of ways to change how each one looks. Nearly all of them will allow you to change the display to fit a book-style criteria, and one of the easiest ways to do that is by changing the font to something that looks more book-like.
With a book open, look for the Aa symbol at the top. This will allow you to open the settings for that book, and by navigating to Font Family in the Font menu, you can change it to something that feels more appropriate. If you want something that is more traditional and less computer-like, a serif font like Baskerville or Palatino will be a great help.
Alter your layout
Combining landscape mode with a two-column layout, which you can turn on by pressing Aa and navigating to Orientation in the Layout tab, can also help make the Kindle feel more like a book with two pages.
Another way to make the layout of each book feel more natural is to go into settings and change the margins and text weights. By widening the margins, therefore narrowing the way your eyes scan each block of text, you can get your Kindle display to have extra space around the edges of the text in the same way a book does. If you combine this with increasing the weight of the text, essentially giving it a bolder appearance by going into the Font menu, it helps make each passage look more print-like.
Change the brightness and warmth settings
If you have a long history of reading physical books, reading a Kindle may be difficult to get used to at first. One of the reasons it feels less like an actual book is the bright, digital screen that you're reading it on as opposed to paper. By adjusting the brightness and display output, you can dial in something more nostalgic.
With a book open, tap the top of the screen, and you'll be given access to the Kindle's Quick Actions menu. Crushing the brightness a bit and then turning the warmth up helps create something that feels a lot closer to a physical book.
Add page-turn animations
Some of you may not be aware of this, but you can adjust how the book is actually consumed minute to minute by turning on page-turn animations, which help to get you closer to the feel of reading an actual book. These aren't supported on every single Kindle, mostly being on Amazon's Colorsoft, Paperwhite and Scribe, as well as mobile versions.
This creates a gentle transition as you tap or swipe between pages. While it doesn't necessarily recreate the genuine, tactile feel of turning a page, it does help to keep the illusion of reading a book at the forefront of your brain. It can really let you sink into whatever you're reading.

title_en: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
title_fa: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
excerpt_en: YC-backed Island turns screen time goals into a farming game, rewarding users with new crops, animals, and more when they stick to their limits.
excerpt_fa: YC-backed Island turns screen time goals into a farming game, rewarding users with new crops, animals, and more when they stick to their limits.
content_en:
A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.
This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft.
Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.
“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.
“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”
With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.
“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.
What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.
Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.
The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.
Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.
Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.
The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.
The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

title_en: Tesla goes all-in on the Cybercab with upcoming €3B Berlin gigafactory expansion
title_fa: Tesla goes all-in on the Cybercab with upcoming €3B Berlin gigafactory expansion
excerpt_en: Tesla is putting Europe on its Cybercab roadmap with a €3 billion expansion of its Berlin gigafactory.
excerpt_fa: Tesla is putting Europe on its Cybercab roadmap with a €3 billion expansion of its Berlin gigafactory.
content_en:
Just two months after putting its first Cybercabs on the road, Tesla is making a multibillion-dollar bet on mass production of the golden-hued, two-seat autonomous vehicles.
The company announced Monday that it will spend €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its Berlin gigafactory, with plans to begin building Cybercabs there in 2029. The new building in Grünheide, just east of Berlin, will be capable of producing up to 1 million vehicles per year, André Thierig, Tesla’s senior director of manufacturing for the site, wrote on LinkedIn.
Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The expansion will make the facility the most technologically advanced of all Tesla factories, Thierig added.
Tesla has been directing more resources toward the Cybercab project, a reflection of its mission to become an AI and robotics company, rather than just an automaker.
The company has already announced plans to cease production of the Cybertruck next year, in part to make room for Cybercab manufacturing at its factory in Austin, Texas.
Musk doesn’t see much of a future for drive-it-yourself EVs even though demand for the Model 3 and Model Y has remained strong despite flagging U.S. sales. The company delivered more than 486,000 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the second quarter. Sales in Europe have been rising as EV adoption continues apace.
Musk has been far more interested in pushing the company toward fully automated driving systems that don’t require a human driver to pay attention — unlike the company’s current advanced driver assistance system, known as Full Self-Driving (Supervised).
The steering wheel-free Cybercab, which was first revealed in 2024 and launched publicly in September, is the current centerpiece of that plan. It’s notable for its lack of a steering wheel, pedals, and other traditional motor vehicle equipment, some of which is required under federal safety standards. (Federal regulators are currently investigating Tesla’s self-certification of the vehicle.)
Tesla’s approach to self-driving systems differs from that of competitors such as Waymo. Tesla relies solely on cameras, rather than additional other sensors such as lidar, to help provide its self-driving system the means to understand its environment. Camera data mimics human vision, but without sufficient training, AI models can struggle to interpret situations that additional sensor data might help clarify.
Tesla has so far taken a slow approach to its Cybercab rollout. The vehicles have been restricted from driving late at night, though Tesla has been working to extend their operating hours. In the more than two months that Cybercabs have been operating, they haven’t had any major incidents.
That track record appears to have given Tesla enough confidence to commit significant resources to expanding Cybercab production and availability. Tesla has about 1,307 robotaxis registered in Texas. Most are modified Model Y vehicles that are used in robotaxi services in several Texas cities. But the Cybercab numbers are growing with about 573 on roads in Austin and soon Dallas.
Now, Europe is firmly on its roadmap, too.

title_en: You won't find Nothing phones at US carriers, but here's how you can still buy them
title_fa: You won't find Nothing phones at US carriers, but here's how you can still buy them
excerpt_en: While you can't get one at an AT&T or Verizon store, Nothing has partnered with Best Buy.
excerpt_fa: While you can't get one at an AT&T or Verizon store, Nothing has partnered with Best Buy.
content_en:
You won't find Nothing phones at US carriers, but here's how you can still buy them
While you can't get one at an AT&T or Verizon store, Nothing has partnered with Best Buy.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Nothing is bringing its latest Android smartphone to the US market, hoping that a minimalist aesthetic, strong camera and a low price entice American buyers away from Apple, Samsung and Google. Technically advanced for an entry-level phone, the Nothing Phone 4a Pro made waves when it was released in March 2026 alongside the company's latest line of headphones. Despite the excitement, spurred by a slick new design and a marketing campaign headlined by brand ambassador and shareholder Charli XCX, Americans have had trouble getting their hands on the cyberpunk smartphone.
Nothing's lack of American market penetration can be chalked up to a variety of factors. For one thing, the startup relied on a beta-program to sell and test its Phone 3a, Phone 3a Pro, and CMF Phone 2 Pro stateside. Moreover, the London company has yet to open a brick and mortar shop in the continental US, although it plans to launch a flagship store in New York City in the near future. This lack of visibility in American storefronts makes it difficult for shoppers of unlocked cellphones to directly compare the startup's offerings with its competitors. And although the firm states that its American online sales are on the rise, its yet to experience a breakthrough.
The greatest hurdle, however, may be Nothing's approach to phone carrier partnerships. To date, the company has yet to strike a deal with American carriers like Verizon, AT&T or T-Mobile. This is an acute challenge for American buyers, since most purchase their phone through their carriers. However, this doesn't mean that getting your hands on the startup's new smartphone, the Nothing Phone 4a Pro, is impossible.
Getting your hands on a Nothing phone
In June 2026, Nothing struck a deal with Best Buy to bring its Android phones and audio gadgets to more than 500 stores across the country. For those not within spitting distance of these select Best Buy locales, you can find the company's phones, headphones and earbuds on Best Buy's website.
Prior to its deal with Best Buy, you could only purchase Nothing's products online, either through the company's Amazon store or its official website. But thanks British company's first brick and mortar retail deal in the US, you can now walk into an American storefront and try a Nothing phone for yourself. The move could be a major boon for the startup, allowing potential customers to directly compare Nothing's cyberpunk aesthetics to its competitors. And although Nothing's US sales grew steadily over the past calendar year, the latest venture into storefronts could further establish the chic minimalist startup on the American phone scene.
As it stands, Nothing offers two smartphones to American audiences: the Nothing Phone 4a Pro and Nothing Phone 3. The former, released earlier in June 2026, is an affordable midrange smartphone with a bold design, strong battery life, a decent camera and an updated version of the company's popular Glyph Matrix. The Nothing Phone 3, meanwhile, is a more powerful phone built for an AI-heavy experience. Powered by Snapdragon's 8s Gen 4 processor, it delivered a significant performance jump from Nothing's previous models. However, it is also significantly more expensive. Crowned as the company's "first flagship" phone, it is an enticing option facing stiff competition.

Nothing's bring your own device (BYOD) approach is great for those seeking flexible, budget friendly carrier options. Although not available to purchase through an existing carrier, Nothing gives buyers the flexibility to choose the network that is best for them.
One strong option would be signing up with a mobile virtual network operator, or MVNO, which lease access to larger carriers' networks like AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile for a cheaper price point. Plans with MVNOs like Mint Mobile, US Mobile and Google Fi offer affordable plans that you can easily connect to your new minimalist smartphone.
Those looking for the reliability of a major carrier can opt to sign up for a plan with AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. However, some plans are more difficult to setup than others. For one thing, the Nothing Phone 4a Pro's Amazon page warns against linking the unlocked phone with any of Verizon's networks. Of course, linking a Nothing phone to a Verizon it isn't impossible, just inconvenient. To do so, Verizon must manually add your phone's IMEI number to its database. According to some reviews, customers found the process of doing so difficult. Notably, Nothing doesn't guarantee full network performance on Verizon's networks.
To avoid the hassle, you can limit your search to T-Mobile, AT&T and MNVOs utilizing their mobile networks. For more information on Nothing's US compatibility metrics, visit the company's support page.

title_en: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
title_fa: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
excerpt_en: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.
excerpt_fa: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.
content_en:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

title_en: GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty to stealing and leaking gameplay footage
title_fa: GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty to stealing and leaking gameplay footage
excerpt_en: Arion Kurtaj was deemed fit to stand trial earlier this year after breaching Rockstar's systems in 2022
excerpt_fa: Arion Kurtaj was deemed fit to stand trial earlier this year after breaching Rockstar's systems in 2022
content_en:
GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty to stealing and leaking gameplay footage
Arion Kurtaj was deemed fit to stand trial earlier this year after breaching Rockstar’s systems in 2022
A hacker who attempted to extort Rockstar Games after breaching the developer's systems and procuring early gameplay clips of Grand Theft Auto 6 has pleaded guilty to several charges, according to the BBC.
Arion Kurtaj, 21, targeted Rockstar in 2022 while on bail for other attacks, including hacking NVIDIA. While under police protection from rival hackers, Kurtaj carried out the phishing attack on Rockstar with the help of an Amazon Fire TV Stick he plugged into a hotel room TV. He procured dozens of clips showing almost an hour of unfinished GTA 6 gameplay. After failed attempts to extort the developer, Kurtaj released the footage as well as some source code.
In 2023, doctors deemed Kurtaj unfit to stand trial due to his acute autism. After a jury determined he had committed the crimes, a judge sentenced him to an indefinite hospitalization. However, Kurtaj was moved to a standard prison in January after being deemed fit to face trial.
At Woolwich Crown Court in London on Monday, Kurtaj pleaded guilty to the Rockstar hack. He also admitted to other crimes he committed as a teenager while part of the Lapsus$ hacking group, including an attack on Uber. Kurtaj will be sentenced at a later date. A second teenage Lapsus$ member was found guilty in the original 2023 trial and sentenced to an 18-month youth rehabilitation order. That hacker, Thalha Jubair, was sentenced to five years and six months in prison earlier this year for subsequent cyber crimes.
Rockstar said it cost $5 million and thousands of hours of workers' time to recover from the 2022 hack. Until Kurtaj leaked the footage, it had been a secret that one of the playable characters in GTA 6 (whom we now know to be Lucia) would be a woman, the first proper female protagonist in the series.
Rockstar enacted stricter security measures in an attempt to prevent additional leaks, including a ban on developers working from home. However, another leaker started releasing GTA 6 gameplay videos over the summer, which Rockstar described as "heartbreaking." One video that the hacker released last month included story spoilers for the game, which is out on November 19.
The GTA 6 turmoil didn't end there for Rockstar. Reports emerged last week of people being able to shine a flashlight into boxed versions of the game and read the download code that's printed on the inlay (these game boxes include a digital download code rather than a disc). Meanwhile, Rockstar workers are currently voting on whether to unionize.
