title_en: 10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes
title_fa: 10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes
excerpt_en: Apple Notes can be much more than a place for random scraps of information once you learn everything it's capable of.
excerpt_fa: Apple Notes can be much more than a place for random scraps of information once you learn everything it's capable of.
content_en:
10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes
Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.
For most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live. If you've only used it for basic text, you've probably missed how Apple has added new features to the mix that can solve complex equations, draw graphs, transcribe audio and turn your doodles into images. iOS 27 brought even more, including smarter Siri integration and divider lines, so the app is more capable than ever.
A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended. On the iPhone, that means the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and any iPhone 16 model or later. Those features are flagged along the way, along with anything that requires a specific version of iOS.
1. Math Notes turns Notes into a calculator and graphing tool
The Notes app has a calculator hiding inside it, with the math happening while you're typing. Since iOS 18, when you type an equation and add an equals sign, Math Notes fills in the answer on the spot. It also works with variables, so if you write "dinner = $42" and change that value later, every result that uses it updates automatically. That makes it a surprisingly easy way to split the bill or plan a monthly budget.
Math Notes can do more than give you simple answers. After you type an equation that starts with "y =", tap the equals sign and choose Insert Graph to plot what you've typed right inside the note. If you change the variable, the graph changes automatically to match. It's a neat tool for students to check their homework without a dedicated graphing app.
2. Notes can scan your documents and supports signatures
If you don't have a physical scanner at home, there's no need to download a dedicated scanner app to replace it. Tapping the attachment button in any note shows the Scan Documents option, where Notes will capture a page automatically, including cropping and straightening it for you. The scanner also offers a flash option and image filters if needed.
In Auto mode, you don't even need to tap on the shutter button; the system captures the document once it detects the page's edges and you're holding your iPhone steady. You can scan multiple pages into a single document, which is useful for contracts, lease agreements or anything else that runs longer than a page.
If the document needs a signature, open the scan, tap Markup, then go to Add > Signature. Use a saved signature or draw a new one with your finger, then resize it and drag it into place. It's an easy way to sign and send a form without taking a printout of the pages. Scans are saved to the note as PDFs, which you can annotate.
3. Notes can record and transcribe lectures and meetings
Notes can double as a recorder: choose Record Audio in any note to record and transcribe everything your phone hears. The transcript is searchable, so you can jump into the relevant part of a long lecture instead of scrubbing through the entire session. On iPhone models with Apple Intelligence, Notes can summarize entire recorded lectures or meetings. Phone calls you record also land in Notes inside the Call Recordings folder with a transcript.
The iPhone already has a dedicated recording app in Voice Memos, so it's worth knowing when to use which. Notes is the better pick when the recording is part of something bigger. For a class or a meeting, for example, you can type your own notes, add photos of the whiteboard and keep the recording all in the same note. Everything stays together, so you won't have to switch between multiple apps when you're going through your notes at home. Meanwhile, Voice Memos makes more sense when the audio itself matters most, like an interview you plan to edit or share.
4. Image Wand turns your rough sketches into real images
If you need some help when drawing, sketch something rough with the Markup tools, then pick Image Wand from the same tool palette and circle your sketch. Add a few words describing the image you want, and Apple Intelligence will turn your doodle into a polished image.
You also have the option to circle an empty spot in the note and create a new image based on the text around it. Afterward, fine-tune the image by adding or removing descriptive words. If your note is a packing list for a beach trip, for instance, it will generate a matching seaside illustration to sit at the top.
In iOS 27, Image Playground, which powers this feature in the Notes app, got a new model that can make photorealistic images, not just stylized ones. Since iOS 27.2, most images you generate or edit carry a SynthID watermark, which the SynthID detection website uses to know something was made by AI.
5. Shared notes turn Notes into a family to-do list
Your notes don't have to be only for you; it's possible to share a specific note or an entire folder with your family, friends and coworkers, then everyone can make changes in real time. This is ideal for a household grocery list or a group plan for a trip. The person who creates the shared note remains in control of who can do what.
Just tap the Share button in the note you want to add people to, then choose whether each person can make changes or only view it. Type @ followed by someone's name and they'll get a notification pointing them to the note. If several people are editing the same note, the activity view and highlights show who changed what and when. And in iOS 27, the Shared folder now sits at the top of the folders list with a new icon, so multi-person notes are easier to spot.
6. Apple Intelligence can summarize, reformat and proofread your notes
The Notes app can help with the actual writing you do. Select some text, tap the Apple Intelligence button in the toolbar and pick an option from the Writing Tools menu. This can proofread your text for spelling and grammar mistakes and rewrite it in a friendlier, more professional or more concise...

title_en: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?
title_fa: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?
excerpt_en: Tired of watching your phone's battery jump from green to red? It's time to start troubleshooting what's causing your battery percentage to suddenly drop.
excerpt_fa: Tired of watching your phone's battery jump from green to red? It's time to start troubleshooting what's causing your battery percentage to suddenly drop.
content_en:
What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?
An aging battery or a recent software update could be the reasons behind your phone's sudden battery drops.
Few things are more frustrating than noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster than usual. It gets to a point where it can no longer last a full day away from the charger. Under normal conditions, battery drain depends on what you're doing on your phone. Lighter uses like browsing the web and listening to music use less power, while taking lots of photos and playing games tend to drain your battery faster. But when your phone's battery suddenly drops without heavy use, something might be wrong.
At the same time, that doesn't mean your phone's battery is dying. Software can also cause your battery to drain faster, like when you install an iOS or Android update, or when an app is constantly running in the background. If you've been noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster, here's what you can try to fix it.
Why your phone battery percentage suddenly drops
Your phone doesn't know exactly how much charge is left in the battery. In fact, it estimates that number based on the battery's voltage and current, and sometimes that estimate is far off from reality. Eventually, the software recalculates it, and that's when you see the battery percentage suddenly drop by a significant amount instead of gradually. This happens more often with batteries in poor condition. As lithium-ion batteries age chemically, they no longer retain their full charge capacity and may also fail when the phone needs a power boost to perform a demanding task, like opening the camera or using GPS. As a result, your phone may think the battery is much lower than it actually is.
Smartphones have mechanisms to prevent this from happening. On iPhones, Apple has implemented a system that detects when the battery fails to reduce performance in order to avoid these spikes in power consumption. Temperature also has a major impact, as most phones are rated to operate at temperatures between 0° and 35° C (32° to 95° F). Using your phone at temperatures above that range can significantly reduce battery life. When your phone gets too hot, the battery will most likely drain much faster. It's best to stop using it until it returns to a normal temperature. Don't put it in a refrigerator, though, as the introduction of cold air can create condensation within the warmer phone.
Also, it's perfectly normal to see your phone's battery drain a little faster for a few hours or even days after an update. Both iOS and Android run a series of optimizations to put all the files in their proper places, and this increases battery consumption. The good news is that this is temporary, and everything goes back to normal once the indexing process is complete. A buggy app or a process constantly running in the background, especially if it uses your location, will also drain your phone's battery quickly.
How to fix battery drain issues
Start by closing apps running in the background to see if your battery usage returns to normal. It's also worth taking a look at your privacy settings and limiting access to your location to only when you have an app open. This prevents your phone from constantly triggering the GPS. That alone should have a significant impact on reducing battery consumption. Also, check your phone's battery settings to see exactly which apps are draining your battery the most — both iOS and Android provide details on this.
Pixel 6 and later models have a Battery Diagnostics tool under Settings. On a Samsung Galaxy, open Settings, then Battery and tap View Details. For iPhone users, it's as simple as going to Settings and opening the Battery menu. These menus usually include details about your phone's battery health. Apple, for example, says that the latest iPhones are designed to retain 80 percent of their original battery capacity through up to 1,000 charge cycles. If your phone's battery health is below 80 percent, you should probably replace it with a new one — which, at least, is much cheaper than buying a new phone.

title_en: Here's what actually happens if your laptop battery is completely drained
title_fa: Here's what actually happens if your laptop battery is completely drained
excerpt_en: While letting your laptop run out of battery may seem harmless, it might be doing more long-term damage to your device than you ever expected.
excerpt_fa: While letting your laptop run out of battery may seem harmless, it might be doing more long-term damage to your device than you ever expected.
content_en:
Here's what actually happens if your laptop battery is completely drained
A dead battery might do more damage than you think.
If your laptop has ever run out of battery unexpectedly, you know what an inconvenience it can be — especially if you're out in the world without a charger. One minute you're cranking away on some crucial spreadsheet for work, and the next, you're staring at your own face reflected in a black screen. Aside from the jump scare of the latter, there could actually be a bigger risk to letting your laptop battery completely drain.
Granted, there's a lot of information on the internet about the best ways to take care of your battery. Some of it hinges on the type of battery and how you use it. No matter how you cut it, though, a total drain isn't ideal, even if it won't set off a disaster if it happens from time to time. Nevertheless, here's what happens when you fully drain your laptop battery.
What happens when your battery drains
On the whole, lithium-ion batteries, like those you'd find in a laptop, are pretty low maintenance and have several perks, such as being able to charge fairly quickly. In a perfect world, you wouldn't get all the way down to 0%. HP explains that if you want to extend your laptop battery's life as long as possible, it's best to keep the charge somewhere between 20% and 80%. Others might recommend charging to 40% to 80%. Either way, this also takes a bite out of the myth that you should drain your battery before recharging it in the name of longevity.
Repeatedly letting your battery drop to low levels can cause wear to the battery. Staying within a safe range helps keep the lithium ions in a stable state. Battery degradation could affect charging capacity. It should also be noted that some systems, like Windows, will actually shut down or hibernate before your battery hits 0%.
Factors that might drain your battery faster
If you find yourself flirting with that 0% a little more often than you'd like, it might be worth investigating whether there are reasons your battery is draining faster than normal. Most current laptops will last between 4 and 12 hours on a single charge, with some lasting even longer. This will vary depending on your laptop and what you're doing with it. For instance, gaming laptops won't last as long.
Otherwise, you could have apps running in the background that you don't need. Depending on the laptop you have, you might have some energy options to check out and tweak. Older software, higher temperatures or even plugged-in devices could all be contributing to your battery drain.
In any case, it's worth keeping an eye on how much battery you have left if you're not connected to your charger. On the whole, draining your battery is mostly a self-inflicted annoyance. It's also not something you want to make a regular habit of doing, particularly if you're interested in making your battery last as long as possible.

title_en: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
title_fa: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
excerpt_en: Bharat Semi says it has secured design wins for its AI-enabled sensor technology with companies including General Atomics.
excerpt_fa: Bharat Semi says it has secured design wins for its AI-enabled sensor technology with companies including General Atomics.
content_en:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.
The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.
India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.
The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.
Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.
Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.
The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.
The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.
Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.
“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.
In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.
The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

title_en: Why your Wi-Fi slows down when more devices connect
title_fa: Why your Wi-Fi slows down when more devices connect
excerpt_en: Your Wi-Fi router is like a busy train station, and once you get a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep the incoming and outgoing traffic humming.
excerpt_fa: Your Wi-Fi router is like a busy train station, and once you get a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep the incoming and outgoing traffic humming.
content_en:
Why your Wi-Fi slows down when more devices connect
Your Wi-Fi router is like a busy train station, and once you get a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep the incoming and outgoing traffic humming.
Demands on home Wi-Fi have increased considerably over the past decade, never mind the launch of the first routers way back in the 1990s. It used to be that homes had a handful of connected devices at most, typically big-ticket items like PCs and game consoles. Today, there's a good chance your watch is online too, and that you've got a plethora of cool smart home gadgets ranging from lamps to smart speakers.
That can create a real crunch on performance. But why is that, exactly? You probably know part of the answer, yet there may be more going on than you imagine. Your Wi-Fi router isn't just a series of tubes — a better analogy might be a central train station with complicated lines of incoming and outgoing traffic.
Once you have a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep this congestion under control. It's not just about minimizing the number of connected devices — controlling how and when gadgets connect can also have a substantial impact.
Why Wi-Fi speeds crumble under high loads
All Wi-Fi routers have an internal bandwidth cap, but there are some differences between types of home internet. Wi-Fi 6 and 6E routers top out at 9.6Gbps, whereas Wi-Fi 7 ups the ceiling to 46Gbps. Although you're unlikely to approach even the 9.6Gbps mark, which is well beyond the scope of most internet plans, we should emphasize that these limits represent total available bandwidth — going not just to and from the internet but locally between devices. If someone's transferring a few dozen gigabytes of video from their camera to their laptop, it could create momentary congestion if a bunch of other devices are also trying to run full-tilt.
Complicating matters is the issue of band congestion. Wi-Fi 6 provides 2.4 and 5GHz bands, while 6E and 7 add a 6GHz option. Each band is allocated only so many channels, so if a band fills up, the result is likely to be delays or a kick over to another band, assuming a device supports it and that your router isn't using separate band IDs. The 2.4GHz band is particularly easy to overwhelm, since there are only three non-overlapping channels, and many low-power accessories don't have 5 or 6GHz has a option.
In fact, all routers have an invisible limit on simultaneous connections, which is why you should upgrade immediately if you're still using Wi-Fi 5. That protocol may only be able to handle as few as 10 to 25 active devices, and it's going to boot older connections to make room for new ones once that limit is reached. I learned this the hard way when I started reviewing smart home gear in the 2010s.
What you can do to sidestep Wi-Fi congestion
Upgrading to Wi-Fi 7 may help, but be warned that it's not a magic bullet. It's still possible for a band to become overloaded. To truly take advantage of Wi-Fi 7's features — such as "preamble puncturing," which allows a channel coping with interference to be carved out for its remaining bandwidth — both your router and connecting devices need to support it. Chances are, most of the devices you own are still limited to Wi-Fi 6 or 6E.
With or without Wi-Fi 7, it may help to steer as many devices as possible over to 5 or 6GHz if your router allows the creation of separate band logins. It's a win-win. While those bands have shorter range than 2.4GHz, they offer both less congestion and faster connection speeds for the devices that support them.
That's not an option on mesh routers, however, so you may need to resort to other tactics, such as using your router's app controls to pause unnecessary devices when a particular upload or download is crucial. In the long term, you should consider migrating as many smart home accessories as possible over to hub-based setups, particularly light bulbs. While standalone Wi-Fi bulbs are cheap and easy to set up, each one has to compete for available channels. Conversely, a hub can link dozens of products via protocols like Thread or Zigbee while only demanding a single Wi-Fi connection.

title_en: How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?
title_fa: How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?
excerpt_en: Determining the stamina of your portable power station is more complicated than simply dividing its battery capacity by the power consumption of your devices.
excerpt_fa: Determining the stamina of your portable power station is more complicated than simply dividing its battery capacity by the power consumption of your devices.
content_en:
How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?
Determining the stamina of your portable power station is more complicated than you might expect.
This is anecdotal, perhaps, but based on the number of ads I'm bombarded with, it feels like portable power stations have become a hot commodity in the last several years. And it makes sense — in a society increasingly dependent on phones and laptops, not to mention other electronics, even the best small power banks just won't cut it during a prolonged outage. And of course, these stations have always had uses outside the home, such as camping or job sites.
A critical question to ask is how much power you actually need. More isn't always better, since a high-end station is not only expensive, but considerably larger and heavier. A multi-kilowatt station might cost as much or more than the devices it's powering and require help to lift if you've been neglecting the gym.
Let's take 1,000Wh (watt-hours) as a baseline. How long can you reasonably expect that to last when the power goes out at home or you're watching YouTube in the Adirondacks? The answer is surprisingly complicated. It depends on what you plug in, how it's actively operating, and how efficient your power station is at converting energy.
The real-world limits of a 1,000Wh power station
While there are plenty of options out there from brands like Anker and EcoFlow, let's take the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 as an example. It's rated at 1,024Wh, and can deliver up to 1,500W of output. Simple math suggests that a 200W fridge, for example, could run for over five hours, or that a 65W laptop could last for well over 15 hours.
In practice, however, even Jackery only promises four hours for that fridge and 11 hours for the laptop. So what gives? The answer is power conversion. When you plug into a station's AC outlet, that power has to be converted from DC, possibly wasting anywhere from 5 to 20 percent in the process. Total efficiency is impossible, and you might make things even less efficient if you plug in something like the wall adapter for your phone or tablet, which converts AC back to DC.
It's also worth noting that the rated consumption for devices can vary wildly in practice. A gaming laptop might consume a few dozen watts when it's browsing the web, but well over 200W when it's running full tilt. Even your phone is going to have ebbs and flows, based on what it's trying to do — it takes a lot more more juice to stream a TV show over 5G than it does to add those crackers to your calorie counter.
What you can do to stretch out a power station's runtime
For a start, if a station has built-in USB ports, plug your phones, tablets and other mobile devices into those whenever possible. You'll reduce the inefficiency created by plugging in adapters. Naturally, this also frees up AC outlets, allowing you to plug in other critical gear.
Pay attention to ambient temperatures, too. While something like the Jackery 1000 is rated for output at temperatures from 14 to 113F (-10 to 45C), the optimal range for its LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) batteries is actually around 59 to 95F (15 to 35C). You'll get less power out a battery that's extremely cold or extremely hot, so simply keeping a station in the shade or properly ventilated could make a world of difference.
In the long term, consider the impact of charging cycles. There's a difference between battery capacity and battery life, and as with any rechargeable battery device, the usable capacity of your portable power station shrinks over time, based largely on how many full cycles (or their equivalent) you've gone through. It may be hard to put a dent in something with a kilowatt-level supply, but that should be a reason to avoid draining a power station unless you really need it.

Total efficiency is impossible, and you might make things even less efficient if you plug in something like the wall adapter for your phone or tablet, which converts AC back to DC.
It's also worth noting that the rated consumption for devices can vary wildly in practice. A gaming laptop might consume a few dozen watts when it's browsing the web, but well over 200W when it's running full tilt. Even your phone is going to have ebbs and flows, based on what it's trying to do — it takes a lot more more juice to stream a TV show over 5G than it does to add those crackers to your calorie counter.
What you can do to stretch out a power station's runtime
For a start, if a station has built-in USB ports, plug your phones, tablets and other mobile devices into those whenever possible. You'll reduce the inefficiency created by plugging in adapters. Naturally, this also frees up AC outlets, allowing you to plug in other critical gear.
Pay attention to ambient temperatures, too. While something like the Jackery 1000 is rated for output at temperatures from 14 to 113F (-10 to 45C), the optimal range for its LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) batteries is actually around 59 to 95F (15 to 35C). You'll get less power out a battery that's extremely cold or extremely hot, so simply keeping a station in the shade or properly ventilated could make a world of difference.
In the long term, consider the impact of charging cycles. There's a difference between battery capacity and battery life, and as with any rechargeable battery device, the usable capacity of your portable power station shrinks over time, based largely on how many full cycles (or their equivalent) you've gone through. It may be hard to put a dent in something with a kilowatt-level supply, but that should be a reason to avoid draining a power station unless you really need it.

title_en: Samsung is discontinuing these useful mobile apps in December
title_fa: Samsung is discontinuing these useful mobile apps in December
excerpt_en: You don't have long to grab the augmented reality tools for your Galaxy devices.
excerpt_fa: You don't have long to grab the augmented reality tools for your Galaxy devices.
content_en:
Samsung is discontinuing these useful mobile apps in December
You don’t have long to grab the augmented reality tools for your Galaxy devices.
Samsung is yanking a couple of augmented reality apps that some folks might find handy from the Galaxy Store. If you're interested in snagging Quick Measure or AR Doodle for your Galaxy devices, it's best to do that relatively soon as the company will remove the apps on December 31. However, Samsung suggested it may bring them back in the future.
Quick Measure has an apt name. It's a virtual ruler app that allows you to measure distances and areas in meatspace. As for AR Doodle, that enables you to sketch on and add 3D effects to photos and videos.
Samsung has posted similar notices of termination on each app's store listing. It said that, after December 31, "new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it is already downloaded, but please be aware that some features may not function properly." The company added that they won't get compatibility updates for future versions of its operating system. So, updating your device's OS once we're into 2027 could break Quick Measure or AR Doodle.
"We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause," Samsung added. "We are committed to returning with improved services in the future." The company hasn't shed any light on when Quick Measure or AR Doodle might return, or if it will move their features into other offerings.
As long as you're quick on the draw, you can download Quick Measure and AR Doodle to compatible devices from Samsung's Galaxy Store.

title_en: How one 13-year-old is helping solve a huge solar panel limitation
title_fa: How one 13-year-old is helping solve a huge solar panel limitation
excerpt_en: This teenager's affordable DIY solar panel design is attracting national attention, and for good reason.
excerpt_fa: This teenager's affordable DIY solar panel design is attracting national attention, and for good reason.
content_en:
How one 13-year-old is helping solve a huge solar panel limitation
Tired of moving solar-powered Christmas lights, a seventh grader built a tracker that lets gravity do the work.
Jason Chang was sick of his mother asking him to adjust the family's solar-powered Christmas lights to get more sun, so he devised a solution with big potential. The 13-year-old seventh grader at Worcester Academy in Massachusetts created a solar tracker that utilizes water and gravity to move a solar panel without the need for a motor, a sunlight sensor or electricity to power the mechanism.
The prototype was less than $25 and generated about 20 percent more voltage than a stationary panel in outdoor tests, CBS Boston reports. The contraption tackles a basic limitation of fixed solar panels: the inability to change position as the sun moves across the sky. This teenager's bright idea is attracting national attention. Here's how it works.
A bucket of water does the heavy lifting
Chang's invention is similar to a seesaw. A small solar panel is mounted on a rotating wooden structure, with water dripping into a bucket on one side. The frame tilts the panel throughout the day as the bucket fills, increasing its weight. There's no sensor needed to determine the sun's position, and the drip rate is adjusted to keep the panel tilting at approximately the correct speed.
It's not difficult to get the process started. Simply pull the plug to set the water in motion. However, it took a lot more work to get that flow just right. Chang spent over a year refining the project, jotting down his tests in a notebook and using recycled materials for much of the construction. And while gravity is free of cost, trying to make it work on a schedule takes a little engineering.
The reported 20 percent improvement also needs to be examined. In the outdoor comparisons, Chang's setup was able to generate higher voltage, but that doesn't necessarily translate to a 20 percent increase in power or total energy output. To calculate those gains, current readings and energy measurements over time would be required, but were not included in the report. It's a positive outcome for a student prototype, but not a guarantee to save you 20 percent on your electric bill.
Why your rooftop isn't quite ready for it
Using water and gravity to follow the sun isn't entirely new. There are commercial trackers on the market that can move with the sun, but they cost more than fixed units. There are also some build-it-yourself designs similar to Chang's concept. Engineering for Change promotes a SunSaluter rotating solar panel kit with a suggested retail price of $50. That cost doesn't include the panel, battery, and other components. Chang's version offers another inexpensive DIY take on the idea, rather than a commercially ready replacement for existing trackers.
There's a practical reason why most rooftop solar panels aren't designed to move around. Trackers can boost energy yields from ground-mounted arrays, but they also add costs and maintenance. It's easy to tilt a small wooden frame, but mounting moving panels on a roof where they have to withstand wind and rain is where it gets complicated. Any extra electricity would have to be worth the investment and maintenance. Another fixed panel might be a lot less hassle for some homeowners.
Sure, motor-free tracking could still appeal to people running small off-grid systems, where every bit of power counts. However, water has its own set of issues. While cold weather can actually boost solar panel efficiency, a mechanism that relies on flowing water has an unwelcome winter issue: ice, which is why Chang is working on a winter version.
CBS did not say how often the water needs to be refilled, how often the tracker needs to be reset, or whether the design has been tested with full-size panels in strong winds. Regardless, Chang's work as a seventh-grader is exceptional. In 2026, he was one of 55 students recognized as National STEM Champions.

title_en: How to get warnings about speed cameras in Apple CarPlay
title_fa: How to get warnings about speed cameras in Apple CarPlay
excerpt_en: Whether you use Apple Maps, Google Maps, or Waze in CarPlay, ensure these settings are on to receive warnings about nearby speed cameras.
excerpt_fa: Whether you use Apple Maps, Google Maps, or Waze in CarPlay, ensure these settings are on to receive warnings about nearby speed cameras.
content_en:
How to get warnings about speed cameras in Apple CarPlay
CarPlay is just the messenger, while your navigation app does all the hard work.
With all the rage and controversy over Flock cameras, speed cameras (or speed traps) have taken a back seat. Most of us have to deal with speed cameras (though they're banned in some states and limited in others), and Apple CarPlay is one way to handle them. While CarPlay itself doesn't send out speed camera warnings, alerts can be turned on for whichever navigation app you use. It stands to reason that Apple CarPlay users default to Apple Maps, but there are other, equally useful alternatives like Waze and Google Maps. There's always a caveat, however. Regardless of the nav app you use, mobile speed traps, by definition, move around a lot. Unless someone reports the new position on a given app, you won't get a warning.
Mobile speed detectors (in some form or another) have been around since the first speeding arrest in the US in 1899. A NYC taxicab driver named Jacob German was caught going 12 mph in an Electrobat (nearly the speed of light back then) in an 8 mph zone. The mobile units in those days were police officers on bicycles. Fortunately, modern technology provides drivers with information as it changes, but there's no such thing as a navigation app that knows where every camera is at all times.
Getting your navigation app to speak up
In Apple Maps, there is no camera switch to toggle on or off. Camera alerts are automatic in supported regions. Waze, a compatible CarPlay navigation app, turns camera alerts on by default. You have the option to fine-tune them as well. In the Waze app, open Settings > Alerts and Reports > Reports > Cameras. Each camera type has its own toggles for "Show on map" and "Alert while driving." Make sure any changes made in the Waze app take place before connecting to CarPlay, because Waze only applies them the next time you connect and go for a drive.
Google Maps is similar yet has slightly different settings. On CarPlay, tap "Report" to pinpoint a mobile speed camera so other drivers can see when using the app. If you want information provided by other drivers, open Google Maps in CarPlay and tap Settings > Alert options > All alerts.
Some navigation apps will send warning alerts without actively navigating, as long as the app is running passively in the background. Radarbot sends alerts for fixed and red light cameras through CarPlay if you have a Gold membership. Roadar adds Flock cameras to the mix, along with other license plate readers mixed in, with speed and red light camera alerts. If you're more concerned about Flock cameras, FlockHopper is free and works with CarPlay as well.
Does Apple CarPlay tell you the speed limit?
It can, though it depends on what navigation app you're using. With Apple Maps, the Speed Limit toggle is in Settings > Apps > Maps > Driving. The posted limit will appear on screen while you navigate. With the Waze app, make sure you're disconnected from CarPlay, open Waze and tap Settings > Speedometer > Show Speedometer > Set Preferences > Show Speed Limit. Google Maps is similar to Waze, with the speed limit located in the speedometer settings. Open the Google Maps app, tap your profile picture and tap Settings > Navigation > Driving > Speedometer.
Stock CarPlay doesn't include a speedometer, but apps like Waze and Google Maps will display current speeds through CarPlay if you want. Both Google Maps and Waze will warn you if your speeds climb too high, and Waze will give you a heads-up if speed limits are about to drop sharply. In response to car manufacturers ditching CarPlay, Apple introduced CarPlay Ultra, which displays your current speed on the instrument cluster, unlike regular CarPlay. CarPlay Ultra is fully integrated, so it's not an informational speed display, as Google Maps makes clear about its own speedometer.

title_en: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
title_fa: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
excerpt_en: "Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia."
excerpt_fa: "Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia."
content_en:
We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”
“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”
Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here.
Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days.
Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.
But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down
Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.
And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.
Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.
But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.
So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.
Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.
Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.
And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.
But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.
Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.
I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.
I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.
Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.
Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.
Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two...

content_en:
I open with this caveat: I haven’t had a ton of time to digest the surprise Armand Hammer record that dropped this week. Billy Woods and Elucid rarely miss, though, and my initial reaction is that Snakes & Ladders ranks among their best. It doesn’t have the seamless throughline production-wise that their collabs with Alchemist (Haram and Mercy) do, but it’s still clearly the singular vision of the two men at its center.
Listen to this: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders
Armand Hammer’s latest album is among their best.
Listen to this: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders
Armand Hammer’s latest album is among their best.
Ominous noises dance in the background, blasts of noise add dashes of industrial rage, bass lines throb, and saxophone bleats call out to the sky. Woods and Elucid have always had excellent taste in production, but here they seem to have brought out the best in collaborators like clipping, Kenny Segal, and Child Actor. They’ve also successfully rallied them around a specific sound palette that keeps the record from actually sounding like it has beats from 11 different producers.
Of course, what makes Armand Hammer stand out from many of their contemporaries is their unique and verbose flows. Their lyrical mastery even makes guest rappers like $ilkmoney, who you can practically hear stalking around the mic as he seethes on “Risk,” up their game.
On songs like “Gravity,” Billy Woods navigates burgeoning romance with shocking directness, while also acknowledging obliquely how hard it can be to say what you mean.
Get it off your chest or put it to the side
As a preface, all due respect, I suggest
‘Cause it’s nothing more precious than time
On “Vespers,” he references Siouxsie and the Banshees and says “My nightcap three fingers of Fernet,” which is probably the first time I’ve ever heard Fernet Branca get a shoutout in a rap song.
“Graveside” is another highlight where it’s Elucid’s turn to get vulnerable:
I see you in the grave, I see you in the dirt
Shouts and hollers every which way, hurting
Darkness chase light
Steel shut close curtain
In some ways, this record feels like a culmination of what Billy Woods and Elucid have been working towards on their non-Alchemist-produced Armand Hammer records like We Buy Diabetic Test Strips, but also their recent solo records like Golliwog and Revelator.
Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Qobuz, and Deezer.

title_en: How to tell whether your car supports Apple CarPlay
title_fa: How to tell whether your car supports Apple CarPlay
excerpt_en: Determining if your car is compatible with Apple CarPlay is quite simple. If yours is not, there are ways to add CarPlay to your vehicle.
excerpt_fa: Determining if your car is compatible with Apple CarPlay is quite simple. If yours is not, there are ways to add CarPlay to your vehicle.
content_en:
How to tell whether your car supports Apple CarPlay
Most newer cars do, but there are a few exceptions.
Apple CarPlay is one of the most useful pieces of in-car software out there, unifying navigation with the other iPhone features you might want to use while driving, like a music player. It's good enough that it can be a selling point to help you decide between two cars when you're looking to buy one. Fortunately, it's extremely easy to tell whether your car supports Apple CarPlay, and there are a few options for integrating it even without built-in support.
Apple maintains a list of every car model that currently supports CarPlay online. The list is extensive, covering basically every new car model from major manufacturers. A few notable exceptions are Tesla and Rivian, which don't support CarPlay at all. GM previously attempted to pull away from supporting Apple's software on newer models in favor of its own version but has since added CarPlay back.
There are also a few ways to check in person if a particular car you're looking at supports wireless CarPlay. With Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on your iPhone turned on, also set the car's dashboard to Bluetooth or wireless. Press the voice command button on the car's steering wheel, then see if the car appears on the list of available devices in Settings > General > CarPlay on your iPhone.
If you can connect your phone to the car's USB port, you'll get a prompt to activate wired CarPlay if the car supports it. You can also check the dashboard screen for a CarPlay option or look for a CarPlay symbol on the USB port, though even supported cars may not have the symbol in every case.
You can still add CarPlay support if it's not included
If you find yourself with a car that doesn't have integrated CarPlay support, there are a few ways you can add it yourself, though not without some hassle and expense. The easier method is to buy a third-party CarPlay screen to add to your car. Made by a variety of manufacturers, these screens can be mounted to your dashboard, essentially replacing your car's existing screen or adding one if you don't have one already. Most brands can interface with both CarPlay and Android Auto, letting you use all the software's functions on any vehicle. They're fairly inexpensive, typically around $100 or less, and can be moved from car to car. The downside is that you'll be relying on an extra piece of third-party hardware, and finding a good place to mount it can be tricky depending on your vehicle.
A permanent but more complicated solution is to install a CarPlay-compatible head unit. This will replace the car's stereo receiver (and screen if your car already has one) with a new screen capable of using Apple CarPlay. This option will likely be more expensive than just buying a screen, though some units can still be found in the $100 range. You'll also have to go through a more complex installation process or pay someone to do it for you, but the advantage is having an integrated unit rather than an extra peripheral to wrangle.

title_en: AO3 is back online but with limited features
title_fa: AO3 is back online but with limited features
excerpt_en: The outage lasted two weeks but full functionality is expected to resume soon.
excerpt_fa: The outage lasted two weeks but full functionality is expected to resume soon.
content_en:
AO3 is back online but with limited features
The outage lasted two weeks but full functionality is expected to resume soon.
After two weeks in the dark, popular fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back online. However, Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit organization that runs AO3, said that some features have been temporarily disabled as a compromise to bring the site back earlier than the four-week mark, according to an update post on the website. OTW said that features like icons and external work importing are currently disabled, while works can only be downloaded in HTML format. The organization clarified that these features will be restored and that no icons have been deleted.
AO3 was taken offline at the end of October due to "evidence of a security incident" that OTW said would result in two to four weeks of downtime. Now that the open-source fan fiction repository is back online, its users may still run into some issues, according to OTW. The organization said it implemented an "intentional measure to help manage traffic," so users may experience delays with the website loading but can refresh to continue trying.
As for the site's data, OTW said that none of it was deleted, adding that user "works, bookmarks, kudos, etc. are still safe." OTW also managed to pause AO3's draft deletion feature so that no drafts were deleted during the downtime. Users should log back in and check on their drafts, though, since the feature will turn back on starting November 29 so that drafts longer than 30 days old will be deleted.
It's still unclear what the cause was, but OTW confirmed it was a "security incident" and that it would "not be sharing specifics about what mitigating changes are being made at this time." OTW added that it partnered with a security firm to review the incident and analyze the site to prevent future incidents. The update post said that OTW has "no reason to believe that the user database was compromised, though we cannot rule out that possibility," recommending that users change passwords, update linked emails and change passwords of any other sites that share a password with AO3 accounts.

title_en: How to get the most protection from your Ring camera security system
title_fa: How to get the most protection from your Ring camera security system
excerpt_en: A Ring camera can provide a huge boost to the safety of your home, but there's more you can do to maximize that added layer of security.
excerpt_fa: A Ring camera can provide a huge boost to the safety of your home, but there's more you can do to maximize that added layer of security.
content_en:
How to get the most protection from your Ring camera security system
Simply putting the camera on your front door may not be enough.
Let's be blunt here. There are good reasons to skip Ring for your home security, from ongoing privacy concerns to some key features relying on a subscription. At the same time, it remains the most practical security platform for a lot of people, at least in the US. That's especially true if your smart home platform of choice is Alexa, which is likewise owned by Amazon.
If you are going to use Ring, it's vital to maximize your setup's efficiency. Some of the company's products can be costly, and your goal here is to deter and record intruders (although you'll need a Ring subscription to do this), not just maintain an illusion of security. If that's all you care about, you might as well slap a few ADT stickers on your home along with a "Beware of Dog" sign.
Efficiency isn't about covering the widest area — it's about thinking like a thief, yet spending as little as possible for the results you need. You also need to be concerned about minimizing false alerts.
The principles you need to know for your Ring system
Your first consideration should be capturing all possible points of entry — and we mean all of them. Don't just position cameras over your doorways. If you've got a side alley, for example, it's possible that an intruder could climb a fence and break in without ever appearing on your door-based video feeds. Give your outdoor cameras overlapping views when possible, and make sure they're installed around 9 feet high, excluding doorbells. This will not only ensure a wide field of view, but make it harder for intruders to smash or tamper with your equipment. That said, cameras should also be easily visible beyond your property. Any halfway intelligent thief is going to think twice if they know they're being recorded.
Ring is eager to sell you indoor cameras, but these aren't actually necessary unless you're hoping to monitor a child, pet or guests. By the time an intruder makes it indoors, all you're really doing is capturing further evidence of their crimes. If you do buy indoor cameras, position them high in the corners for broad coverage, with an eye toward entryways.
Once cameras are in position, be sure to spend time customizing their Motion Zones via the Ring app. This can prevent unwanted motion detection from objects such as passing traffic or trees blowing in the wind. But really, you'll also want to turn on Advanced Motion Detection if a camera supports it, and most importantly, Smart Alerts. These let you narrow alerts to people, packages and/or vehicles, so when you receive notifications on your phone, you'll know to take them seriously instead of tuning them out. Smart Alerts do require a subscription, so remember that before you come to depend on them.
Redundancy can be a lifesaver
A factor that's all too easy to neglect is redundancy. You should always have a backup battery available for your cameras powered by removable batteries, for example, because it can take hours to fully recharge one. You may also want spare cables or installation tools.
Even more critical is the quality of your Wi-Fi network, since you need a stable signal for uninterrupted video. Be sure to test for any weak spots or dead zones, and consider upgrading to a mesh system if you can't fix them with better router placement. You don't need to go with Amazon's eero routers, but if you can't afford any downtime whatsoever, look into models with cellular backup features. These can keep your entire network online at the cost of a monthly fee. You may want power backup too, however, and that can get very expensive on the whole-home level.
Lastly, don't forget to consider supplementing your cameras with door and window sensors (tied to a Ring Alarm system), as well as automatic lighting. While newer Ring cameras do have great night vision, lights from Ring or otherwise can improve video clarity further and make intruders visible to everyone. Just make sure lights aren't blaring into your neighbor's windows or too easily triggered by people passing by.

title_en: Wi-Fi 8 is an attempt to fix the biggest problem with wireless internet
title_fa: Wi-Fi 8 is an attempt to fix the biggest problem with wireless internet
excerpt_en: With current Wi-Fi standards reaching beyond consumer-level speeds, Wi-Fi 8 is entering the fray with a fix that makes those speeds mean something.
excerpt_fa: With current Wi-Fi standards reaching beyond consumer-level speeds, Wi-Fi 8 is entering the fray with a fix that makes those speeds mean something.
content_en:
Wi-Fi 8 is an attempt to fix the biggest problem with wireless internet
Because perfection currently remains just out of range.
Sometimes, better doesn't mean faster. With Wi-Fi 7 realistically capping out at about 23 Gbps (a number virtually nobody will see in the real world), speed is more than covered in the current generation. At this point, the biggest concern is reliability. Released in 2024, Wi-Fi 7 has been known to suffer from pain points like poor stability, weak wall penetration, and relatively short range.
Wi-Fi 8, which is still in development, is designed to address the considerable reliability issues plaguing the internet today. Final approval is expected in 2028, although companies like ASUS and TP-Link wasted no time announcing their first Wi-Fi 8 router based on the draft spec.
Minimizing the rough patches of Wi-Fi
Most home internet plans offer speeds of a few hundred megabits per second, which older Wi-Fi 6 routers should handle with ease. For faster speeds, like a 2 Gbps fiber connection, Wi-Fi 7 can largely keep up (especially if you're sitting right next to the router). Wi-Fi 8 shifts the focus to stability, aiming to plug the holes that lead to shaky connections. It's being designed to fix common issues, like a weak signal in one part of the house, an apartment building with 20 networks competing for airtime or a clunky mesh handoff when walking between rooms.
The underlying standard, 802.11bn, is nicknamed "Ultra High Reliability," accentuating its focus on consistency and stability. Wi-Fi 8 should achieve 25 percent better throughput for weak signals, 25 percent fewer dropped packets (especially when moving between access points) and 25 percent lower latency at the shakiest moments.
The main way it gets there relates to how access points work together. Today's routers share channels by taking turns, and not always in the most efficient manner. Wi-Fi 8 refines that by letting compatible access points coordinate when each one transmits. That will make the most sense with mesh systems.
The catch
Although you can buy an ASUS gaming router or mesh system built on Wi-Fi 8 today, with a TP-Link model coming soon in some regions, they won't make much difference yet. For the upgrades to show themselves, both the router and the device (phone, laptop or tablet) on the other end need to support it as well.
So buying one now is more about investing in the future than some mythical immediate payoff. (Not that you'd know it from the marketing.) And since these first devices are built on a draft spec, there's no guarantee they'll support everything in the final version.
Eventually, Wi-Fi 8 should be worthwhile, especially if you live in a congested building or use a mesh network. Just be prepared to wait a year or two before you reap the benefits. For now, Wi-Fi 7 is still a perfectly reasonable choice for a new router. And if yours isn't positioned ideally, moving it to a central location will likely do more than any new standard, whether draft or final, will

excerpt_en: United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon's competitor to SpaceX's Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a...
excerpt_fa: United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon's competitor to SpaceX's Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a...
content_en:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon’s competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today’s launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA.
Vulcan rocket fails, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload to orbit.
ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload to orbit.
In a statement posted on X, ULA said, “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.”
The company said it was currently unclear what caused the failure, but pledged transparency as it continues its investigation. Amazon projected confidence in its launch partner despite the failure, posting on X that, “ There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01. ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

title_en: Spotting a fake SD card is easier than you think
title_fa: Spotting a fake SD card is easier than you think
excerpt_en: Fake SD cards have been a problem for years, but there are some simple steps you can take to protect your wallet and your files.
excerpt_fa: Fake SD cards have been a problem for years, but there are some simple steps you can take to protect your wallet and your files.
content_en:
Spotting a fake SD card is easier than you think
Fake SD cards have been a problem for years, but there are some simple steps you can take to protect your wallet and your files.
If you're in the market for a new SD card, you might want to tread with a little extra caution. Buying a fake SD card online could cause you problems you didn't anticipate when all you wanted to do was save some files.
Fake SD cards might seem like they're everywhere, but they aren't new. You can go back years on forums like Reddit and find people complaining about having been duped by an SD card that was priced in a manner that was too good to be true. As chip and memory shortages drive up prices on HHD, SSD, RAM and more, consumers might be more inclined to snap up an SD card that costs less. A PCWorld article from early 2026 found that compared to 2025, some SD cards have doubled (or more) in price.
While an inflated price tag is a headache, a worse fate might be using a fake SD card only to find valuable files lost, corrupted or overwritten. How-to Geek explained that scammers can make it seem as though a storage device can hold much more than it can. Problems arise when you try to move a file onto a device that just doesn't have the capacity. Fortunately, there are some steps you can take to make sure the card you bought works and your files are safe.
Warning signs
Experts explain that before you buy, there are some warning signs an SD card could be fake. A card that's suspiciously cheap is a big red flag. You might also want to steer clear of SD cards sold by unauthorized third-party resellers on platforms like Amazon or eBay. Additionally, watch out for brands you're unfamiliar with (though some have reported seeing counterfeits using big names or names that mimic the most reputable brands).
You should also inspect the packaging — are there missing labels or a lack of warranty information? Some advise staying away from refurbished cards altogether. If you want to make sure the card you're buying is legitimate, it can't hurt to go to a physical retailer and grab one there. When it comes to preserving your files, taking a chance for the sake of saving money might not be worth the risk.
How to test an SD card
If you want to test an SD card before loading it up with important files, there are some different approaches to take. If you have a Windows computer, you can use H2testw – a free, downloadable program that will help you check both the speed and memory of storage devices like SD cards and flash drives. Its website notes that it was developed expressly because there have been so many instances of bunk SD cards and flash drives. Once you install the program, you can plug in your device, select it within h2testw, and the program can tell you whether the device is functioning properly and whether it has the storage it says it has.
You can also use f3, which stands for Flight Flash Fraud. It's an open-source program that, according to its website, "fills the device with pseudorandom data and then checks if it returns the same on reading." The website also contains detailed directions for how to use the program, depending on your operating system.
Another approach is to check the SD card's performance because slow speeds can be another issue connected to fake SD cards. A program like CrystalDiskMark can help you benchmark an SD card's performance. XDA explains that an SD card will usually have a baseline number of reads and writes displayed somewhere on the packaging. The results of the test should be in that range.
So, the next time you're looking to buy a new SD card, make use of these warning signs and tests to avoid disaster with your files.

title_en: You can control your other devices with this resourceful Apple feature
title_fa: You can control your other devices with this resourceful Apple feature
excerpt_en: There's a lot you can do with this accessibility feature.
excerpt_fa: There's a lot you can do with this accessibility feature.
content_en:
You can control your other devices with this resourceful Apple feature
This accessibility feature can be really useful.
With iOS's Switch Control, you can control your iPhone or iPad using alternate input methods ranging from external adaptive controllers to head movements and hand gestures. It's a useful accessibility feature for anyone with limited mobility that's even more powerful than it might seem at first if you dig into its settings. One option, Use Other Devices for Switch Control, lets you use the alternate controls you set up on one iOS device to control other devices on the same Wi-Fi network, and it only takes a little bit of setup.
First, you need to enable Switch Control across your devices. Make sure any devices you want to control are connected to the same Wi-Fi network and you're signed into the same iCloud account on all of them. If you want to control a Mac desktop computer remotely, you also need to open the Apple menu, click Accessibility and open the Switch Control menu. Select Allow platform switching to control your computer. Then on your mobile devices, open the Settings app, click Accessibility and turn the Switch Control toggle on. Now you can assign external controllers or gestures to specific actions by selecting Add New Switch under the Switches menu and following the onscreen prompts.
Once you have your switches set up, head back to the main Switch Control menu and select Device, then Use Other Device. This will show you a list of all the compatible devices linked to your network. Select one and you can use the switches you've already established to control them remotely. When you want to stop controlling the remote device, just select Stop Using Device under the same menu.
Switch Control is more versatile than it looks
While Switch Control's Use Other Devices feature can only be used to control iOS devices, you can assign non-Apple devices as your external controllers. Adaptive controllers made by other companies like Microsoft can be mapped as switches, but you can even use devices that aren't intended as accessibility tools. Standard game controllers work as well, along with other devices that can connect to your iPhone or iPad via Bluetooth or USB, like Bluetooth keyboards.
Switch Control is intended to make navigating iOS devices and selecting items on screen easier for people with limited mobility, but some users have found novel ways to use it for more than basic functionality. Switch Control lets you set up Recipes, which can be used to record and replay sequences of inputs. With a little work, iOS users have set up Switch Control to automate repetitive actions in mobile games or other apps and to turn pages in the Kindle app. These unintended applications may not always be the best use of Switch Control, but it's worth experimenting with how you can use the feature, especially if you've got multiple iOS devices and want to try controlling them all from one place.

title_en: Jensen Huang might be plotting a return and more of the latest Nvidia drama
title_fa: Jensen Huang might be plotting a return and more of the latest Nvidia drama
excerpt_en: The drama around Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang is evolving quickly. The latest edition of our Stepback newsletter should get you up to speed, but there have already been a number of new developments since this morning. That includes rumors that Jensen Huang might...
excerpt_fa: The drama around Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang is evolving quickly. The latest edition of our Stepback newsletter should get you up to speed, but there have already been a number of new developments since this morning. That includes rumors that Jensen Huang might...
content_en:
The drama around Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang is evolving quickly. The latest edition of our Stepback newsletter should get you up to speed, but there have already been a number of new developments since this morning. That includes rumors that Jensen Huang might be trying to find a path back to CEO, and a statement from Megaspeed claiming that Alice Huang hasn’t worked for the company since August of 2025, which raises more questions than it answers.
Jensen Huang might be plotting a return and more of the latest Nvidia drama
Megaspeed claims Alice Huang hasn’t worked there since August of 2025.
Megaspeed claims Alice Huang hasn’t worked there since August of 2025.
- Some big names, including Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, have publicly thrown their support behind a public letter demanding Nvidia “bring Jensen back.”
- The public letter calling for Jensen Huang to be reinstated has over 150,000 signatures, but it’s difficult to verify their authenticity. Business Insider reports that signatures include “Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor” and “Xi Jingping,” likely a misspelling of Chinese president Xi Jinping.
- The Financial Times reports that Jensen Huang has discussed the possibility of returning as CEO with close allies, as some Silicon Valley insiders and employees attempt to pressure the board.
- Not all believe Jensen Huang should be allowed to return to his seat. According to the Financial Times, one ally acknowledged that, “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense.”
- 23andMe founder Anne Wojcicki told Bloomberg that “Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible … We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable.”
- Wojcicki endured a messy public split from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, as their separation in 2013 became public along with the news that he was romantically involved with a Google employee, before their divorce settlement was finalized two years later.
- According to Bloomberg, many women in Silicon Valley see Jensen Huang as simply another example of a rich man abusing their position and “leveraging power to pursue sexual relationships with their employees.”
- Megaspeed released a statement saying that Alice Huang left the company “effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” adding that “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”
Correction, November 15th: A previous version of this article described Brin’s reported relationship with a Google employee as an affair, updated to clarify that it was reported after he and Wojcicki separated.

title_en: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
title_fa: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft
excerpt_en: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
excerpt_fa: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
content_en:
While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.
Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.
In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”
Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night.
“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday. When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”
“Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”
